narrationScript: While declaring variables like `struct Student s1;` is perfectly functional, repeating the `struct` keyword can make your code a bit verbose and less concise. To address this, C provides the `typedef` keyword. `typedef` allows you to create an alias, or an alternative name, for an existing data type. When used with structs, it can dramatically improve code readability and make your custom types feel more like C's built-in types. You can use `typedef` in two primary ways with structs. First, you can define an anonymous struct—meaning it doesn't have a tag name—and immediately assign an alias to it. So, you would write `typedef struct { ... } Student;`. Now, `Student` is an alias for this specific struct definition. Alternatively, if you still want to keep the struct tag name for other reasons, you can use `typedef` to create an alias for that tagged struct. For example, `typedef struct StudentTag { ... } Student;`. In both cases, the result is the same: you can now simply use `Student s1;` instead of `struct Student s1;` to declare a variable, making your code much cleaner and easier to read.
